sent.t: Seven handbags.
That is how many were hanging behind my door in Kyoto the year I turned 60.
Seven.
And six of them were quietly adding years to my face.
It is not because I am thinner than you.
I am five feet tall and I am not a model.
It is not because I am richer.
It is the weight, the strap, and where the bag sits when I talk to somebody.
The safe advice says, buy one good black bag, put your whole life in it, and match it to your shoes.
I did that for years.
That advice is the reason I look tired in every photograph from that time.
The last one on this list is the one nobody in America talks about, because it is not about buying anything.
It is about a box in a closet, and at the end you will know exactly what to change tonight, with the bags you already own,
nothing to buy.
My mother, Fumiko, was a kitsukeshi in Jion.
She dressed brides and geiko in kimono for 40 years, from 1965 until her hands gave out.
I also lived 19 years in California, in Sunnyvale from 1983 to 2002 because my husband Hiroshi was an engineer there.
So I know your closet.
I had the big American bag too.
I did it the American way.
Mistake one, the bag that carries the whole house.
Carol Whitfield is my best friend from Sunnyvale.
She is 70 now.
She lives in Sacramento, and she calls me every Sunday night, which is Saturday morning for her.
In September, she told me she bought a new bag for her trip.
She was very proud of it.
I asked her to put it on her kitchen scale, empty.
4.6 pounds, empty.
That is a bag that has already decided how your day will go.
My neighbor, Mrs.
Kinoshita, is 81.
She walks 10,000 steps on the philosopher's path every morning.
Her bag weighs 11 ounces.
I have weighed it, because she let me, and then she laughed at me.
Here is the part nobody says.
The bag does not have to hurt to change your face.
When I carried four pounds on my left side, my shoulder rolled forward, my chin came forward to balance it, and my whole face went down
with it.
In photographs, I looked like I was listening to bad news.
I was not.
I was carrying my umbrella, my water, my papers, and a book I never opened.
So, before I go on, stand up, I will wait.
Put your bag in one hand, Arm straight down at your side and count to 30 out loud.
Then do the other arm.
If one arm wants to drop before 30, that bag is not your bag anymore.
Nothing is wrong with you.
The bag is heavy.
A change.
Empty it on the table tonight and weigh it.
Under 2 pounds empty.
Mrs.
Kinoshita's rule and now mine.
If it does not fit in the bag, it goes in the coat pocket.
Mistake 2.
The bag on one shoulder with the strap that slides.
You know this one.
The strap slips.
You lift your shoulder.
It slips again.
You lift again.
Sachiko-san, who owns the cleaners on the corner of my street, told me in February that I shrugged 11 times while we talked.
She counts things.
She once told Hiroshi he had worn the same cardigan for three days and she was right.
Eleven times in one conversation.
That little shrug is the gesture of a tired woman.
It is not the bag that looks tired.
It is you doing that all day.
After 60, my shoulder is not a shelf anymore.
The strap has nothing to sit on, so it slides, and I spend the whole day holding it up with my neck.
The change is a strap across the body, not on the shoulder, across.
The bag sits at the hip in front, and it does not move.
If your bag has no long strap, a strap extender is about $12, and any bag can take one.
I moved a strap on three of my bags and I did not buy a single new bag.
Tonight, put it across, walk to the kitchen and back, and lift both arms above your head.
If the bag stays where it is, keep it that way.
Mistake 3.
The bag carried in the hand or hanging from the crook of the elbow.
This This is the one I see most in America, and it is the one that ages the hand.
A bag hanging from two fingers pulls the tendons up, the veins come forward, and the whole arm hangs straight down like it is tired of
you.
In June, we have the rainy season here, Tsuyu.
I was at the station stairs behind Mrs.
Kinoshita, and she had an umbrella in one hand.
Her bag was across her body, so her other hand was free for the railing.
Behind her, a woman my age had a bag hooked on her elbow and an umbrella in her fist, and she had to stop at the
top to change hands.
Mrs.
Kinoshita went down those stairs like a girl.
The change, a thin strap, 47 inches, worn across.
If the bag came without one, Daiso sells a clip-on strap for about $9, and I have three of them in different colors.
My mother wore kimono, so she carried her things in the obi.
Her rule was simple.
The hands are for the hands.
Tonight put the bag on, then open a door, hold a cup, and pick up a shoe from the floor.
One hand free.
That is the whole test.
The bag you cannot close.
An open tote is a beautiful thing in a photograph and a bad thing at the Nishiki market on a Saturday.
Mr.
Okada sells fabric and a tanugi in Nishiki.
I have known him since I was a girl because my mother bought lining silk from his father.
In November, I was at his store, and he said to me, in Japanese, the open bag is an invitation.
He said it quietly, the way he says everything, and then he went back to folding.
Two weeks before that, my phone slid out of my own bag at Kawaramachi, and a schoolgirl ran after me with it.
I did not even feel it go.
That is the part that stays with me.
I did not feel it.
After sixty, we carry more, not less, the glasses, the second pair of glasses, the keys, the tissues, the paper with the address.
And we look down less, because looking down is a decision now.
An open bag is a bag you are trusting everybody else to be kind about.
The change, a zip or a flap.
If your bag has neither, put everything in one small zip pouch inside it.
Nine dollars.
And in a crowd, wear the bag in front with your hand on the zip, not behind you.
In front, like a small animal you are carrying.
Tonight, reach behind your back without looking.
If your hand finds an open top, that bag is for the garden, not for the train.
Mistake 5.
The black bag held up at your face.
Here is what my mother did with every bride in Gion.
Before the bride left the room, Fumiko held the edge of the obi up under her chin, and then she walked her to the window.
Not to the lamp, the window.
She said a color must be tested where the real light is, because a color that is beautiful under a bulb can be a gray line
under the chin at noon.
A bag held under the arm or a clutch at the chest is that test.
It is a block of color right under your face, and most of us choose black, because black is safe and it goes with everything.
After 60, the color leaves my face before it leaves my hands.
Everyone tells me this is rude to say It is not rude, it is just true And it means black under my chin Takes the last
of the light with it The change Hold the bag low, at the hip Where it is not part of your face Or choose a warm
colour, camel, mustard A dull red, like the maples in November I do have a black bag It hangs at my hip, and it stays there
Tonight, stand at the window with the bag under your chin.
Then lower it to your hip.
Look at your face, not the bag.
You will see it in ten seconds.
Mistake 6 The little clutch with no strap At sixty-eight, your hands are busy in a way they were not at forty.
There is the railing.
There is the umbrella.
There is the tray at a party.
There is a grandchild's hand and you do not want to be the grandmother who cannot hold it because both hands are full.
Last December, I was at a wedding in Gion at a reception where everybody stands.
A woman my age held a small clutch under her arm for four hours.
She never once used her left hand.
She could not hold a cup and a bag at the same time.
So she put the cup down, picked up the bag, put the bag down, picked up the cup.
All evening.
Nobody said anything.
Everybody saw it.
The change.
A small bag with a thin strap that crosses the body.
About $18.
Or a chain you add to the clutch you already own.
A small bag with a strap is a big bag with free hands.
Tonight, put the clutch on, then open a door, then hold a cup, then pick up a shoe, all with one hand.
Mistake 7.
The good bag in the box.
This is the one nobody in America talks about, and it is the one I want you to hear.
My mother had a small black leather bag with a brass clasp bought in 1978 in Gion.
She kept it in a box in the Ossiri with a sachet of dried camellia, and she wore it four times a year, a wedding, a
funeral, the New Year, and once, I remember, to the dentist.
When she died in 2009, I opened the box.
The leather had a crack across the flap, a real crack, like a dry river.
Twelve years in a box with a sachet, and the bag had dried out, waiting for a good day.
I carry it now, every day, to the market, to the post office, to the train.
We save the good things for a special day.
And after 60, we learn that the day you can walk to the market is the special day.
So before the last part, if this has been useful, press like.
It tells Yui which videos to keep making.
And she is the one who films me.
So be kind to her.
The change.
Take the bag out of the box tonight.
A little neutral cream, $9.
dollars, the kind for shoes, rubbed in with a cloth.
Wear it tomorrow morning.
Not to a wedding, to the market.
Seven mistakes and none of them needed a new bag.
One, the bag that carries the house, weigh it.
Two, the strap that slides, put it across.
Three, the bag in the hand, Free your hands.
The open bag.
Close it and wear it in front.
Black under the chin.
Hold it low or choose a warm color.
The clutch with no strap.
A thin strap, $18.
The good bag in the box.
It is for tomorrow morning.
Do not buy anything.
Open your closet and put the seven bags on the bed and let three of them go.
Not because they are bad, because they are not yours anymore.
My mother used to say, if it does not make you stand straight, it does not belong to you.
She said it about kimono.
It is the same for a bag.
The right bag makes you stand straight, and then your face does the rest.
Tell me in the comments what is in your bag right now, all of it, including the thing you have been carrying for a year and
never used.
Yui reads them to me with my tea, and I answer the ones about the box.
And next week, Carol is coming to Kyoto in April, and she called me about the subway map.
She could not read it, with the glasses she bought at the drugstore for $12.
So next time, I will take you with me to my optician in Sanzhou, and we will try five pairs on my face, one by one,
in the window light.
My mother's rule about color works for glasses too, you will see.
